column3: Near-verbatim parallel: disbelievers see the messenger and turn his commission into mockery.
What they mocked returns as an enclosing consequence, extending the focus's derisive stance toward accountability.
Earlier messengers are mocked and the mocked matter overtakes the mockers, directly generalizing the focus scene.
Challenges reliance on any force apart from the Most Merciful and names the disbelievers' delusion.
Immediate antecedent establishes the messenger's mortality, the premise from which the surrounding hostile response proceeds.
The remembered fish in the travel narrative does not clarify selective remembrance, mockery, or disbelief.
Positive counterpoint: hearts find reassurance in remembrance of Allah, unlike the focus's refusal of the Merciful's remembrance.
Immediate continuation records the same opponents derisively demanding the promised event.
Defines the revelation as a reminder for all worlds, clarifying the public character of the dhikr the focus rejects.
The demanded matter appears near and disgraces disbelievers, giving a consequence horizon to their taunting speech.
Denial of signs and mockery render faculties useless when the mocked consequence encloses its agents.
Remembering Allah's name in a dietary rule is a distant positive use of remembrance.
Directly portrays taking a known divine sign as mockery and assigns humiliating punishment.
Immediate context frames human life as testing and return, supplying the seriousness beneath the focus's ridicule.
God's sufficiency against mockers directly addresses the pressure imposed by mockery of the messenger.
The opponents call for defending their gods, closely matching the focus's hostile concern for their gods.
Immediate later parallel: messengers are mocked and the mocked matter overtakes those who deride them.
It joins disbelief with making both divine signs and messengers objects of mockery, then states the consequence.
Disbelievers dispute falsely to dislodge truth and take signs and warnings in mockery, directly expanding the focus behavior.
Mockery of believers becomes a distraction from God's remembrance, explaining one way ridicule displaces dhikr.
Turning from remembrance characterizes a worldly orientation, a broad counterpart to the focus's disbelief in the Merciful's remembrance.
Leaders urge persistence with their gods when challenged, a close social parallel to the focus's idol-defensive response.
Immediate context promises signs despite impatient demand, continuing the exchange behind the opponents' taunt.
Those reminded do not remember, providing a compact counterpart to the focus's refusal of the Merciful's dhikr.
Its general disbelief in the hereafter does not develop the focus's mockery or remembrance contrast.
Immediate continuation exposes the disbelievers' inability to ward off the fire they provoke by their demand.
It explicitly describes disbelievers rejecting the arriving reminder, closely matching the focus's disbelief in dhikr al-Rahman.
Obstructing Allah's path and denying the hereafter only broadly resembles the focus's refusal.
The threatened harm encloses Pharaoh's people, a consequence-pattern parallel without the focus's mockery.
Treating religion as mockery and play extends the public social form of the focus's derision.
Immediate continuation names turning away from the remembrance of their Lord, directly restating the focus's final clause.
The promised event arrives suddenly and overwhelms them, continuing the warning response to their challenge.
Mockery is alleged in response to a command, but the episode lacks the messenger-directed derision and idol conflict.
The command not to abandon their gods vividly parallels the focus's defensive attachment to false gods.
Acknowledges the constricting effect of hostile speech on the messenger, supplying the human pressure behind mockery.
It states the recurrent pattern that every messenger is mocked by the criminals.
Refusal even to recognize or bow to the Most Merciful closely counters the focus's disbelief in His remembrance.
The evil of their deeds and the matter mocked both come upon them, clarifying mockery's reversal.
It forbids treating divine signs as mockery, though its legal setting is distinct from the focus scene.
Bare denial by disbelievers supplies no focused account of mockery, idolatry, or remembrance.
Immediate continuation denies that their gods can protect even themselves, directly answering their idol-defensive posture.
After denial, the reports of what they mocked come to them, directly tracing ridicule toward realization.
The growth of inward impurity and death in disbelief does not add a focused neighbour relation.
Making Allah's signs mockery is given as the reason for an inescapable final consequence.
It presents mockery as the recurring reception of every arriving prophet.
The servants of the Most Merciful answer ignorant address peacefully, an indirect contrast to the focus's hostile speech.
Immediate context attributes their false security to prolonged enjoyment, framing the confidence behind their taunt.
Voluntary remembrance is only a general positive counterpart to the focus's refusal.
Benefiting from a reminder supplies only a broad contrast to refusing remembrance.
It opens the nearby sequence characterizing the later mocker as a lying, sinful person.
The command for abundant remembrance of Allah is a direct positive counterpoint to disbelief in the Merciful's dhikr.
Obstructing Allah's path and rejecting the hereafter is only a broad refusal pattern.
Immediate continuation defines the messenger's warning as revelation and depicts unhearing response to warning.
It limits the messenger's role regarding the demanded timing to giving reminder, directly relevant to the surrounding taunt.
Night and day enable remembrance and gratitude, but do not develop the focus's conflict.
The command to proclaim openly and turn from associators supplies the messenger-side response to idol-defending mockery.
The teacher's deferred explanation in a travel narrative does not clarify the focus's remembrance or derision.
Joseph's rejection of an unbelieving people's way is only a remote religious contrast.
Immediate continuation records their admission of wrongdoing when even a slight punishment touches them.
It warns that worldly concerns must not distract from Allah's remembrance, a positive counterpart to the focus's displaced dhikr.
Its affiliation with disbelievers and enduring punishment lacks the focus's mockery or remembrance relation.
Moses's admission about an earlier act is unrelated to the focus.
Remembering Allah after fear in prayer is a distant ritual use of remembrance.
The contrast between the learned and those who remember is too general to clarify the focus scene.
Immediate continuation establishes exact, comprehensive reckoning after the opponents' challenge and mockery.
It directly rebukes claimed play as mockery of Allah, His signs, and His messenger.
Wisdom and remembrance by people of understanding are only a general positive contrast.
Pharaoh's reminder of Moses's upbringing does not illuminate the focus's response to a messenger.
Messengers bring clear proofs, self-satisfied opponents mock them, and the mocked consequence encloses them.
The Most Merciful's ordered creation does not materially clarify disbelief in His remembrance.
Moses's fear of being called a liar is a broad messenger-rejection parallel without mockery or idolatry.
Turning away from the Lord's remembrance is tied to ascending punishment, closely supporting the focus's final refusal.
Frequent remembrance of Allah in places of worship is a distant positive counterpart.
The collapse of a plotters' structure does not clarify mockery, remembrance, or the focus's idol conflict.
Preventing Allah's name from being remembered identifies active obstruction of dhikr, a structural contrast to the focus.
Generic punishment of disbelievers supplies no focused account of their mockery or selective remembrance.
The mention of mercy to Zechariah is a narrative heading, not a neighbour of the focus's dhikr contrast.
Disbelievers react to hearing the reminder with hostile looks and call the messenger mad, closely paralleling messenger-directed contempt.
The command to remember Allah and not disbelieve directly reverses the focus's disbelief in the Merciful's remembrance.
It recalls rejection when called to faith and the later recognition of divine hatred, giving a broad accountability parallel.
The evil end is tied to denying and mocking Allah's signs, directly extending the focus's derisive disbelief.
Disbelievers use a dismissive theological retort to evade an ethical command, a related pattern of resistant speech.
Voluntary remembrance alone offers only a general contrast.
Clear recitation is answered by claiming the messenger seeks to turn people from inherited worship and by calling truth magic, closely paralleling the focus's idol-defensive mockery.
Prescribed remembrance during pilgrimage is a distant ritual counterpart.
Listening to the messenger only to dismiss his speech illustrates resistant reception, though without the focus's mockery.
The instruction to mention Abraham in the Book does not clarify the focus's conflict.
A new reminder from the Most Merciful is met with turning away, directly paralleling disbelief in His dhikr.
Redirecting remembrance from ancestors to Allah loosely contrasts inherited loyalties with the focus's attachment to gods.
Taking beings besides Allah as allies is an indirect idolatry parallel, without the focus's speech or remembrance contrast.
The reaction to a claim about the Most Merciful does not address the focus's mockery or remembrance.
The movement of mountains is unrelated to the focus.
Revelation to the messenger is general background but does not develop the opponents' response.
Satan's withdrawal from a battle scene does not clarify the focus's mockery or idolatry.
Teaching by the pen is unrelated to the focus.
A messenger's appeal to evidence and reform is a remote parallel to public prophetic address.
Lot's call to reverence does not supply a focused neighbour relation.
Destruction of an ungrateful prosperous town gives only a remote consequence context.
The earth's obedience to its Lord is unrelated to the focus.
The request for skilled magicians in Pharaoh's narrative is unrelated to the focus.
They deny the truth when it reaches them, and the reports they ridiculed will come to them; this closely extends the focus's taunting reception.
It consoles the messenger that deniers' speech grieves him while identifying their rejection as denial of Allah's signs.
The people reject exclusive worship of Allah because it would require abandoning what their fathers worshipped, directly paralleling idol-defensive resistance.
Disbelievers answer the messenger's warning with the charge that he is an obvious magician, a direct form of messenger-directed dismissal.
When clear verses are recited, opponents demand a different Quran or its alteration, showing resistance to the messenger's announced revelation.
Mockery directed at Noah during his visible mission is answered with the promise that the mockers will know their consequence.
Shuayb's people derisively ask whether his prayer commands abandonment of ancestral worship, closely combining prophetic contempt and idol loyalty.
A messenger is declared unintelligible and socially weak, a direct hostile reception though without the focus's remembrance contrast.
Disbelieving peoples challenge their messengers and accuse them of trying to turn them from ancestral worship, a near parallel to the focus's defense of gods.
When asked what the Lord revealed, deniers recast it as tales of the ancients, a related dismissive response to revelation.
Private hostile speech calls the messenger a bewitched man, directly showing contemptuous reclassification of his message.
People reject guidance because they object that Allah sent a human messenger, closely paralleling the mockery of his commission.
Clear signs are met with claims of superior wealth and status, showing a social strategy for dismissing revelation.
Pharaoh labels Moses's signs magic and accuses him of seeking to expel the people, a direct hostile recasting of prophetic warning.
A newly arriving reminder from the Lord is heard while the audience plays, directly clarifying the unserious reception behind the focus's mockery.
The opponents secretly reduce the messenger to an ordinary human and call his message magic, immediately framing the focus's hostile speech.
Abraham publicly challenges his people's attachment to statues, directly exposing the idol loyalty defended in the focus.
The idolaters answer Abraham's critique by questioning whether he is serious or playing, a close mockery-and-idolatry parallel.
Abraham announces action against their idols after they turn away, extending the surrounding conflict over the false gods named in the focus.
Abraham exposes the idols' inability to benefit or harm, directly answering the opponents' concern for their gods.
The rebuke of worshipping what cannot benefit or harm directly judges the false allegiance defended in the focus.
A people dismiss their messenger as merely human seeking superiority, a recurring form of resistance to prophetic address.
Another ruling group dismisses its messenger as a human seeking superiority and rejects the promised return.
Disbelievers call the Quran a fabrication aided by others, directly illustrating the false characterization of revelation.
They object that the messenger eats and walks in markets, closely paralleling contempt for his ordinary human status.
They accuse the messenger of following a bewitched man, another direct form of public derision.
They demand angelic encounter or direct vision of the Lord rather than receive the messenger's warning, extending rejection through impossible demands.
They use the Quran's gradual revelation as an objection, directly recasting the messenger's received message as defective.
They say the messenger nearly turned them away from their gods, the closest missing parallel to the focus's grievance that he mentions their gods.
Pharaoh calls Moses a mad messenger, directly exemplifying contemptuous dismissal of a prophet.
Pharaoh threatens Moses with imprisonment if he takes another god, making false-god loyalty an instrument against prophetic speech.
When clear signs come, Pharaoh's people call them manifest magic despite inward certainty, joining recognition, denial, and hostile reclassification.
Clear signs are called invented magic and unheard ancestral novelty, a close parallel to rejecting revelation to protect inherited religion.
Abraham's people answer his argument only with a call to kill or burn him, showing violent defense of idolatry.
The messenger is accused either of inventing lies about Allah or of madness, directly matching derisive public rejection.
A people reduce their messengers to ordinary humans and deny any revelation, closely paralleling the focus's mockery of a human envoy.
The threatened stoning of messengers shows escalation from denial to coercion against their warning.
It laments that every messenger who comes to people is mocked, directly generalizing the focus scene.
The prophet's wonder is answered by the opponents' mockery, a direct messenger-versus-mocker scene.
Seeing a sign only intensifies their mockery, closely linking signs, sight, and derision.
They refuse to abandon their gods for a mad poet, directly combining attachment to gods with contempt for the messenger.
The disbelievers wonder at a warner from among themselves and label him a lying magician, closely paralleling the focus.
Their astonishment that the messenger makes the gods one directly identifies the idol conflict underlying their rejection.
They dismiss the monotheistic call as an unprecedented contrivance, a direct ancestral-defense response.
Mention of Allah alone repels their hearts while mention of beings besides Him pleases them, directly illuminating the focus's asymmetric remembrance of gods and the Merciful.
Pharaoh classifies Moses as a magician or liar, directly representing hostile recasting of a messenger.
People reject messengers because they are human and deny their warning, closely paralleling contempt for an embodied prophetic envoy.
Disbelievers call for obstructing and drowning out the Quran, making public resistance to its hearing explicit.
They persist in their ancestors' way even when a messenger brings better guidance, directly extending inherited-idol resistance.
When truth reaches them, they call it magic and reject it, a direct counterpart to the focus's mockery.
They turn away from the messenger and call him a taught madman, directly combining rejection and contempt.
A person hears Allah's verses, persists arrogantly as though he never heard them, and is promised painful punishment; this closely develops the focus's refusal of dhikr.
Disbelievers are rebuked for arrogant response when Allah's verses were recited, directly linking recitation, mockery, and disbelief.
When clear verses are recited, the arriving truth is called manifest magic, a direct rejection of revelation.
Even after seeing a sign, they turn away and call it continuing magic, closely joining sight and mockery.
Noah is called mad and rebuffed, directly extending the repeated contempt for messengers.
Thamud reject following a human from among themselves, a close human-messenger objection.
The opponents call the Quran inherited magic, directly reclassifying the revealed reminder in derision.
They reduce it to human speech, a direct denial of its divine source.
When Allah's verses are recited, they are dismissed as tales of the ancients, a direct formulaic rejection of revelation.
Their failure to prostrate when the Quran is recited supplies a bodily form of refusal toward the revealed reminder.
